newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwandans ordered out of homes of returned refugees.
newsitem.headline: Rwandans ordered out of homes of returned refugees.

text.p: Rwandans living in houses owned by Hutus who have come back home fleeing fighting in Zaire must move out under a 15-day deadline set by the government, officials said on Wednesday.
The deadline gives as many as 100,000 Hutu families a chance to take back homes they abandoned during civil war and genocide in 1994, said Deputy Rehabilitation Minister Christine Umutoni.

The mainly Tutsi Rwandans who had moved into the houses will be given 15 days to move out after people fleeing the fighting in eastern Zaire register with officials that they are the rightful owners of the houses.
In an effort to lessen the upheaval, the government has offered new plots of land to those who have to move out and was due to start a house building programme on Thursday.

"The principle is returning refugees have a right to their property and the government has a right to enforce it," Umutoni said on Wednesday, nearly three weeks after the start of a flood of hundreds of thousands of Hutu refugees returning from Zaire.

"The aim of the house-building programme is not for people to wait for government to build houses for them but to foster a spirit where people will not leave vulnerable groups stranded on the hillside," she said.
But aid workers fear the deadline could exacerbate ethnic tensions heightened by the sudden return of the Hutu refugees.

"In some communities you have a lot of genocide survivors and a lot of the people coming back participated in the genocide, so with a housing conflict on top you could see a rise in tension," said an aid worker.

A total of 630,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees returned home from camps around the eastern Zairean city of Goma between November 15 and 19 and trekked to their home communes, according to U.S. army figures.

Around two years ago an estimated 800,000 members of the Tutsi minority that was forced into exile in 1959 returned home mainly from Uganda after Tutsi rebels took over Kigali following the 1994 slaughter of Tutsis by Hutu militia.
Rwanda last month appealed to donors for up to $7 million to resettle returnees.
The returnees also need medicine, food, seed and farming equipment, the government says.
Most of the Goma returnees went to Gisenyi, Ruhengeri and rural Kigali provinces but problems were also expected in towns where property ownership was less clear cut, Umtoni said.
The aid worker reported cases where genocide survivors had been forced to live in the same houses as alleged killers.

He said the survivors complained the government, which took power after the victory of Tutsi rebels who defeated the Hutu troops and militiamen responsible for the genocide in 1994, was favouring the Hutu returnees.
"The government is bending over backwards to assist the returning refugees, even sometimes at the expense of other sectors of society," said Gerald Gahima, a top official in the justice ministry.
An estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates were killed in the genocide and two million Hutus, many of them fearing reprisals for the mass slaughter, fled to Zaire, Tanzania and Burundi.
